title: Module 5: Heat Stroke and Cold Injuries (Gulf Focus)
learningObjectives: Distinguish between heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke — and treat each correctly
Recognise that heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate cooling
Apply the Gulf construction heat stress management protocol for preventing heat illness
Understand the pathophysiology of why heat stroke kills
Know the first aid for hypothermia and frostbite in cold storage environments

content.text: The Gulf Heat Emergency — Why This Module Is Critical

Heat illness kills workers every summer in the Gulf. Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, and Oman regularly record ambient temperatures exceeding 48–50°C with radiant heat from the sun and hot surfaces pushing the effective heat load even higher. The Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index — which combines temperature, humidity, radiant heat, and wind — frequently reaches dangerous levels from May through September. For a first aider working on a Gulf construction or oil and gas site, heat illness response is the most likely life-threatening emergency you will face.

All Gulf countries enforce summer outdoor work bans: Saudi Arabia (12:00–15:00, June 15–September 15), UAE (12:30–15:00, June 15–September 15), Qatar (10:00–15:30, June 1–September 15), Kuwait (10:00–15:00, July–August), Oman (12:30–15:30, June 15–September 15), Bahrain (12:30–15:00, June 15–September 15). Even outside these hours, WBGT-based work/rest schedules must be applied.

Painful muscle cramps (usually legs, abdomen) caused by salt and fluid loss during heavy sweating. The worker is conscious, alert, and sweating heavily. First aid: move to shade or cool area; rest; provide cool water with electrolytes (sports drink or oral rehydration salts); gentle stretching of the affected muscle. The worker should not return to heavy physical work in the heat that day.
Heat exhaustion is caused by significant fluid and salt loss. The body's temperature regulation is struggling but not yet failing. The worker is conscious but feels unwell.

items: Signs: heavy sweating; pale, cool, clammy skin; rapid, weak pulse; normal or mildly elevated body temperature (up to 40°C); headache; dizziness, weakness, fatigue; nausea; muscle cramps

First aid: move immediately to shade or air-conditioned environment; lay down and elevate legs; remove excess clothing; cool with cool water spray, wet towels to skin, or fan; give cool water or electrolyte drink if fully conscious and able to swallow; monitor closely — if condition does not improve within 30 minutes or deteriorates, treat as heat stroke and call emergency services

content.text: Heat stroke occurs when the body's thermoregulatory system fails completely — core body temperature rises above 40°C (104°F) and the body can no longer cool itself. Without rapid treatment, heat stroke causes multi-organ failure and death. Heat stroke has a mortality rate of 10–50% even with treatment. It is a medical emergency equivalent to cardiac arrest.

Heat stroke is an immediately life-threatening emergency. Call 911/999 immediately AND begin aggressive cooling simultaneously. Every minute of delay increases brain damage, organ failure, and mortality. Do not wait for emergency services before starting cooling.

items: Signs: high body temperature (above 40°C / 104°F); HOT skin — may be DRY (classic heat stroke) or WET (exertional heat stroke in outdoor workers); confusion, altered mental state, agitation, bizarre behaviour, slurred speech; loss of consciousness; seizures; rapid, strong pulse initially; eventually cardiovascular collapse

content.text: The key difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke: in heat exhaustion the person is still sweating and conscious (but unwell). In heat stroke, thermoregulation has FAILED — they may stop sweating, their core temperature is 40°C+, and they have altered mental state or unconsciousness. Heat stroke IS life-threatening; heat exhaustion is serious but not immediately fatal.
Heat Stroke First Aid — COOL FAST

items: Move to coolest available location immediately — shade, air-conditioned vehicle, cool room
Ice immersion (most effective if available): immerse the casualty in ice water up to the neck — this is the fastest cooling method and saves lives; do not hesitate if ice is available
Ice packs to neck, armpits, and groin — where large blood vessels are close to the skin
Fan with cool air while spraying cool water on the skin
Wet towels or cool cloths over the body, changed frequently
Do NOT give fluids to a confused or unconscious casualty — aspiration risk
If conscious and improving: cool electrolyte fluids sipped slowly
Monitor temperature if a thermometer is available — target below 39°C before stopping aggressive cooling
Recovery position if unconscious but breathing; CPR if cardiac arrest

content.text: A scaffold erector collapses on a Saudi construction site at 14:30 in August. He is hot to touch, confused, and not responding normally. His skin is flushed and still sweating but minimally. Temperature measured: 41.2°C. Action: one colleague calls 911 immediately; two colleagues carry him to the air-conditioned site office; remove his hard hat, vest, and outer clothing; apply ice packs from the site medic's bag to his neck, armpits, and groin; fan him while spraying cool water; monitor every 2 minutes. Ambulance arrives 12 minutes later — temperature has dropped to 40.0°C. He survives with prompt treatment. The same delay of even 15 minutes of active cooling could have resulted in fatal organ failure.

For Gulf construction first aiders and HSE officers, preventing heat illness is the priority. Key prevention measures: WBGT monitoring; work/rest schedules starting from WBGT 28°C; acclimatisation of new workers (7–14 days); 250ml cool water every 20 minutes (not just 'water available'); shaded rest areas with seating close to work area; buddy system so symptoms are spotted early; pre-employment medical screen for heat-vulnerable conditions (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, certain medications).
Cold Injuries in Gulf Industrial Settings

Cold injuries are less intuitive in a Gulf context but do occur. Cold storage facilities (food warehouses, LNG facilities, pharmaceutical cold chains), high-altitude work in Oman's Hajar Mountains in winter, and night shifts in desert areas where temperatures can fall below 10°C in winter are all contexts where cold injury can occur. LNG (Liquefied Natural Gas) facilities present a specific cryogenic burn hazard — LNG is stored at -162°C and contact causes immediate frostbite.

rows: Shivering (mild); confusion, no shivering, muscle stiffness (moderate–severe); unconsciousness (severe)
Remove from cold; remove wet clothing; wrap in blankets; warm the core (not limbs first); warm sweet drinks if conscious; hospital urgently for moderate/severe
Skin white/waxy, hard, numb initially; upon thawing — red, blistered, extremely painful
Protect from further cold; rewarm ONLY if no risk of refreezing (refreezing causes worse damage); immerse in warm water (37-40°C); do not rub; hospital for assessment
Immediate white, waxy freeze burn; can appear similar to heat burns once thawed
Flood with warm (not hot) water immediately; treat as deep burn; hospital urgently — cryogenic burns are deeper than they appear

content.text: LNG cryogenic burns are a specific hazard at Oman LNG, ADNOC LNG (Abu Dhabi), and QatarEnergy North Field LNG facilities — some of the world's largest LNG producers. Workers handling LNG must wear cryogenic PPE (face shield, cryogenic gloves rated for -196°C, thermal coveralls) and must know the first aid response for cryogenic burns. The response (warm water irrigation) is counterintuitive — the instinct is to use hot water, which must be avoided as it worsens the injury.
